feedback: If a learner thinks the predator always wins: point out that many hunts fail (for many predators, most do), often because prey defences work, which is why those defences keep mattering.

If a learner treats all predators as chasers-and-biters: highlight the trap-builder (spider web), the ambusher (crocodile), the cooperators (wolf pack) and the tongue/venom user, none of which rely on raw speed.
If a learner says warning colours help prey hide: correct this — bright warning colours ADVERTISE that an animal is toxic or dangerous (like a poison dart frog), the opposite of camouflage.
activities.intendedInsight: Hunting and defence often come in matched pairs — many attacking tricks are met by defences that work against them — so 'predator' is not just 'fast and toothy' and prey are far from helpless.
learnerActions: Lay out cards or a board with predator strategies on one side (ambush, pursuit, pack-hunt, trap/web, tongue/venom) and prey defences on the other (camouflage, speed/agility, armour/spines, warning colours, herd/group living, confusing patterns).

For each pairing, say out loud who you think usually prevails and why, then check: ambush often succeeds against a dozing, inattentive grazer; staying alert and vigilant makes an ambush less likely to succeed; armour or spines can put off a single biter; a cooperating pack can overwhelm a lone defender, while bunching together in a group helps prey resist a pack; speed is often answered by agility and sharp turns.

Match at least three hunting strategies to the prey defence that works against each one, and name a real animal example for both sides (e.g. crocodile ambush at the water's edge vs an alert, watchful herd; cheetah pursuit vs a gazelle's speed and swerves; wolf pack vs musk oxen that bunch together in a defensive group; spider web trap vs an insect that detects and avoids the strands; a chameleon's long sticky tongue vs insects that are camouflaged or stay hidden; a lone biter vs a porcupine's spines or a skunk's spray; a chasing predator vs zebra stripes, which some scientists think may make a running herd harder to pick out, though this is still debated).
activities.title: Hunt-or-hide matchup: pair each strategy with its counter

feedback: If a learner says the eye-catching dots were 'unlucky': agree that luck plays a part for any single dot, but reframe the pattern as a survival disadvantage — being easy to spot made those dots more likely to be caught.
Connect the result forward: the surviving (hidden) individuals are the ones that pass their colour on, so the next generation tends to be better hidden.
activities.intendedInsight: Camouflage gives a real survival advantage, and because the better-hidden individuals survive to reproduce, their colouring becomes more common over generations — the raw material of the arms race.
learnerActions: Spread coloured paper dots (or sweets) over a patterned cloth — some dots matching the pattern, some standing out clearly.
Before playing, predict out loud which colours will survive and which will be grabbed.
Acting as the 'predator', take 10 seconds to grab as many dots as you can, then count which colours were left behind.

Discuss: compare your result with your prediction. If the well-camouflaged dots mostly survived, then, if these were real prey, the hidden ones would be more likely to live and have young that inherit their colouring. If they did not, talk about why (for example, the time limit, or how the dots were spread out).
activities.title: Camouflage grab game: why hidden prey survive

feedback: If a learner assumes camouflage always means prey: show the ambush case where a predator uses it to stay hidden until the last moment.

Note the limit of a still picture: it shows hiding well, but the actual contest between hiding and being spotted plays out through alertness, movement and survival over generations, which the camouflage grab game and the arms-race ladder explore.
activities.intendedInsight: The same trick — blending into the background — can serve either the hunter (ambush) or the hunted (hiding), showing camouflage as a tool both sides can use.
learnerActions: Look at a scene (a drawn or photographed picture) where an ambush predator OR camouflaged prey is hidden against a matching background.
Point to where you think the hidden animal is, and say which clues gave it away.

Say whether this is a hunting advantage (the predator stays unseen until it strikes) or a defence advantage (the prey stays unseen so it is not found), and explain which side camouflage is helping in this picture.
activities.title: Spot the hidden hunter (and hidden prey)

feedback: If a learner calls the predator cruel or evil: establish that it hunts to eat and survive; both sides are simply surviving, so there is no good or bad.
If a learner says one side wins forever: reconnect to the arms-race ladder — a win just pressures the other side to improve.
Note the limit of a sort: grouping animals by method can check and surface the classification but does not by itself build the escalation intuition; use the story and ladder for that.
activities.intendedInsight: Predation is feeding and survival, not malice, and the two-sided pressure means neither side holds a lasting advantage.
learnerActions: Sort a set of animals by how the predators hunt (ambush / pursuit / pack / trap / tongue or venom) and by how the prey defend (camouflage / speed / armour or spines / warning colours / group living).
For each predator, say why it hunts — to eat and survive — and judge the claim 'the predator is a bad animal for hunting' (it is not; hunting is how it feeds).
Answer and justify: why does no side win permanently? (Because every improvement on one side pressures the other to improve across generations.)
activities.title: Sort and explain: checking the pairings and the 'no villain' idea
